title_o: Modeling distributions of immediate memory effects: No strategies needed?
verdict_reason: The script reads osf.io/srnvg = Dataset/rawdata_preprocessed.zip: 15 tab-separated files, 80 trials each. The per-subject proportion of words in correct order (English lists, short vs long) feeds a one-sided paired t-test, which recomputes to t(14) = 0.496, p = .314, d = .13, matching the table exactly with N = 15.

data_files.notes: 15 files (1.txt..15.txt) x 80 trials; columns list (EN/NL), trnr, length (1 short / 2 long), nr_correct (0-8), W1-W8, w1-w8, rt1-rt8, R1-R8. Trial-level.
Downloaded, listed only: 15 .txt plus __MACOSX resource forks; the unprocessed version.
Variable definitions; demographics (eng, age, gender, lang) are not in the files and are typed into the audit script by hand.

key_test.test: paired t-test, one-sided (greater), mean nr_correct/8 per subject for English short vs English long lists; d = t/sqrt(n) via compute.es

recompute.method: python recomputation (pandas groupby per file, scipy ttest_rel greater)

obstacles: subject id comes from file order, not from a column; the R script's list.files order (1,10,11,...) mislabels the hand-typed demographics, which does not affect the key test
the key test uses only the English lists (pr[,1] vs pr[,3]); the Dutch lists are a second condition a reproducer could pick by mistake
R script needs compute.es; not run
